rv.q: Within the four-square premise the level of invention and precision in this slapstick is often staggering.
What to impart without spoiling the fun, which is considerable and of which there’s no let-up across two hours, plus interval?
The whole barmy enterprise is profoundly silly — and may be too long, at two-and-a-half hours — but I was absolutely taken out of myself for the duration.
It's an amiable show that makes good use of audience participation and neatly skewers the more ludicrous reaches of the magic industry.

At its best, the production carries off some baffling tricks, not least a protracted routine in which an unfortunate artiste is locked tight in a water tank while a ham-fisted conjurer tries to complete a card trick.
It's an utterly (but not fussily) democratic show where everyone gets their moment in the sun and all dignity is sacrificed in favour of laughs.
A fun night out, then – even if the chainsaw that slices Sophisticato’s mother in two is the closest it ever gets to a cutting edge.
They’re both winsome and limited, and ‘Magic Goes Wrong’ feels caught at a strange crossroads between Mischief’s bumbling Englishness and Penn & Teller’s edgier interjections.

But, though it doesn’t hit the highs of some previous Mischief outings, it remains a solidly entertaining show, from a company evidently keen to test itself, and, for once, there are a few sweet instances where everything goes right.

Anyone with a sense of humour is likely to have a wonderful time and could well be exhausted by the end of an evening strong on running gags during which they will find themselves laughing for the vast majority of the time.
Magic Goes Wrong makes for a night of sure-fire entertainment.

But if the company is in imminent danger of becoming a franchise, it's great first of all to see so many of the original Mischief team reunited onstage, which in addition to the writers also includes the comically invaluable (and insane) Dave Hearn, Nancy Zamit and Bryony Corrigan.
There's much to enjoy here, particularly in the interaction with the audience, and despite one or two second-half longueurs Adam Meggido directs with aplomb.

Those who love the 'Goes Wrong' brand will have a pleasant number of laughs to keep the mirth coming, but it's hard to shake the feeling that, for a large portion of the run-time, Mischief may have missed a trick.
It's a consistently funny night out with some impressive conjuring thrown in.
The comedy is broad as the M25 and the plot is about as directionless. But it is also very funny.
The premise is simple, unoriginal and, in their expert hands, often blissfully funny.
This epically scaled and delightfully nightmarish production manages to conjure up uproarious laughter while pulling off some clever tricks of its own.

cn.t: Mischief Theatre's formula of elaborate disasters delivers consistent laughs but feels increasingly familiar. The Penn & Teller collaboration adds impressive illusions, though critics note it lacks the narrative drive of earlier hits.
